lesson.title: The Tinderbox of Europe: Alliances, Empires, and a Single Assassination
lesson.summary: A web of military alliances, imperial rivalries, aggressive nationalism, and an arms race turned the assassination of an Austrian archduke into a continent-wide war within weeks, a war the United States initially tried hard to avoid.
lesson.body:
By the summer of 1914, Europe had been quietly arming itself for a fight for years, even if few leaders expected one so soon. Historians often summarize the underlying causes of World War I with four interlocking forces, sometimes remembered by the acronym MAIN: militarism, alliances, imperialism, and nationalism. Militarism describes the arms race among the great powers, especially the naval competition between Britain and Germany to build ever more powerful battleships, alongside large standing armies and detailed mobilization plans across the continent. Alliances refer to the two rival blocs that had formed by 1914, the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, and the Triple Entente of France, Russia, and Britain, each side bound by treaties to support its partners if attacked.

Imperialism added another layer of tension, as European powers competed for colonies, markets, and resources around the globe, breeding rivalry and suspicion. It is worth noting that the United States was pursuing its own, smaller scale version of this competitive impulse much closer to home, as seen in the Roosevelt Corollary and dollar diplomacy discussed earlier, even as it avoided the kind of entangling alliances that bound the European powers together. Nationalism, the fourth factor, was especially explosive in the Balkans, a region so volatile it was often called the powder keg of Europe. There, various Slavic peoples, including many Serbs living inside the Austro-Hungarian Empire, longed for independence or union with neighboring Serbia, threatening to tear the multiethnic Austro-Hungarian Empire apart from within.

The spark came on June 28, 1914, when Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo, Bosnia, by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist connected to a secret society known as the Black Hand. Austria-Hungary, blaming Serbia for supporting the plot, issued a harsh ultimatum and declared war on Serbia on July 28, 1914. From there, the alliance system did exactly what critics had long feared it might: Russia began mobilizing to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and then France, and when German troops invaded neutral Belgium to reach French territory quickly, Britain entered the war to honor its own treaty obligations protecting Belgian neutrality. Within about a week, a regional crisis in the Balkans had become a continental war involving every major European power.

Woodrow Wilson, discussed in the previous chapter, responded by declaring American neutrality in August 1914 and urging citizens to remain impartial in thought as well as action. In practice, true neutrality proved difficult. American banks and manufacturers extended enormous loans and sold vast quantities of munitions and supplies to Britain and France, tying the American economy ever more closely to an Allied victory even while the government professed neutrality. That uneasy, unofficial partnership would help shape the events of the next several chapters, as the United States drifted step by step toward direct involvement in the fighting.
